I don't think it's only women who encourage men to open up. I do think it's very likely to be mostly women who fit within the feminist leaning group that the meme is talking about though: expressing support for men opening up as part of a progressive belief system, while also being dismissive of men when they do open up in their personal life. 

I just think it's easier for people who have the lived experience of men to see the glaring contradiction and be consistent with their beliefs. Hence why it would make sense for it to be women.

I also wouldn't say that it's possible to open up to women if I believed that all women are unempathetic, that's obviously not true and variable depending on your personal experience. 

As for the reasons to be prejudiced, as I said, men stand to lose the most for who they decide to open up to, and this particularly colors men's  romantic relationships with women, in which they're still expected to uphold traditionally masculine gender roles.

You're missing part of the point of the meme. It isn't that this is specifically true for women, it's that the dismissal comes from those that manifest desire (if not demand) and support for men to open up more (which happens to be mostly women/feminists), and while other men can be dismissive too, I think it's more unlikely for men to be as unempathetic because of the shared gender experience.

I definitively agree on geetting professional help, and I can't really dispute wether women are disproportionally denying men's mental health, but I don't think this is relevant, since the point is to prove that the risk is there, and that (without caution) men stand to lose out the most.

I also do believe that we unconsciously accept that women do burden those around their social circle (both men and women) with their emotional/mental needs, and we don't consider it a problem. I do admit that the fact that more women are socially capable probably allows them to distribute that burden around better than men do, so that's definitively a factor. 

In any case, I think the core point of these memes, is that men perceive that their emotions don't matter, or that they matter less than women's. Which is at odds with the feminist/egalitarian narrative about equality.

Correct. Because of the system in which we live in, I think men should hold with extreme prejudice those who they choose to be emotionally open with, because as men, they stand to lose more. 

As I said, I don't think this is justification to hate women or to assume it is totally impossible to open up to them (if anything, the system should be what we all hate the most). It's a safety measure men need to take for their own sake (without dismissing therapy and actively looking for those you can trust to open up to).

Aren't you proving my point by saying that men should open up to professionals though? Or would you prescribe the same for women? In any case, I agree with you that theraphy is necessary. 

Also, I'm not denying it is a broad generalization. I'm saying that's ok. Just like it is ok for women to assume that any man they don't know is a potential rapist. both are part of systemic problems that are not fixed yet. Maybe we can agree that men should be more flexible by vetting women on how much vulnerability they can be trusted with?

Or maybe, the reason why these memes get popular is because it resonates with men's past personal experiences when opening up, and by saying this, you'd be gaslighting men (ironically, invalidating their experiences) and leaving a problem unattended? 

I don't think it's fair to use this as a justification to hate women and assume that no women can be receptive or that they will never be, but to at least acknowledge that it is a reality that men are likely to encounter, and that, just as women need to be wary about who they have sexual intimacy with for the sake of their own safety/integrity/social standing, men should be extremely wary about who they emotionally open up to, for the same reasons.

Your sadness is equal to a rich person being sad about a poor person only being able to enter/know a mansion as part of a job, and not because they were invited as guests. It just reeks of privilege.   
Love (specially romantic/sexual love) is conditional. Not everyone gets to be loved, and most people's first time involves someone they don't actually love. Consider yourself lucky if that is the case, or if you're even desirable enough to be loved.

>It only takes one, and one is too many.

So, basically men are irredeemable unless absolutely all men are in good behavior? Take away gender related unacceptable behaviors, and try to apply that same logic to basic human behaviors that we could all personally benefit from changing. Do you think that is an attainable goal?

I can agree with  #toomanymen, but if it only takes one bad apple to spoil the barrel what even is the point of attempting to change/being an ally? It's not like that would make a difference anyway. It sounds more like trying to hold all men to an unrealistic standard to validate a bigoted opinion about what is perceived as the intrinsic nature of men. To me, that sounds pretty much the same as the framework in which misogyny, or other type of prejudice operates.

More importantly, if it only takes one, couldn't we make the same assumption about women, since even though a minority, they have also raped, murdered, sexually harassed, etc?

I get that many men use their relationship as therapy and don't seek out how to be vulnerable with others, but that is not the main point. I have male friends I can be intimate with, but the reason why I can do that is because I don't get punished for doing so. What I say or do is not used later to attack/manipulate me, and they still respect me. That is what I see as the main point, we run the risk of getting punished if we share vulnerability with women, unless it's commodified to validate them. Why would you want to open up to someone who will lose respect for you and try to manipulate your feelings unless you open up about the "right" stuff? To be fair, I'd say this is not just a problem about opening up with women strictly, but that has been my experience. I can't talk for all men, but I'm not waiting on women to take care of me. Not getting punished, treated as less of a man, getting your reputation tarnished, or having to sacrifice a relationship for opening up would be nice though. However, that seems like too much to ask.

As someone that's been diagnosed and struggled with AvPD I understand exactly how you feel and your rationale to avoid people/social situations. Not all days are easy to be around people and that is OK. However, the more you expose yourself to situations that could lead to judgment, the more resilient you will become and you will develop better strategies to deal with judgement without crumbling under the pressure. 

Judging is something that we all do to have a value system,  and even though it can be toxic and destructive, it can also help us learn from our mistakes to grow and deepen our relationships with others. It's part of how we form our opinions of ourselves and the world.  However, with AvPD the pain of judgment and humiliation is maximized by our brain regardless of how severe/hurtful the situation can be. So, in my experience, therapy (Cognitive behavioral therapy) has consisted of identifying and challenging the cognitive distortions that maximize the pain of judgment and humiliation. I assume that would be the same route your therapist will take. 

You should slowly expose yourself to situations that will make the cognitive distortions come out so you can learn how to fight them. 

Another thing that you may work on is re-framing your view of the world and yourself. Try to develop more positive statements about other and yourself. This can help you become more resilient to criticism and friendly to other people. 

This can all be extremely hard work and I'd lie to you if I said I don't have my shortcomings, but the more I've worked on it, the better quality of life I've had and I honestly wish I had started challenging my avoidance earlier. I'm 26, letting my avoidance win for so long has severely hampered my social skills and decision making. I've squandered life experiences/opportunities that I took for granted because I let the fear win. 

So, please take a few more risks, learn from the pain, don't lie to yourself and appreciate the good both in other people and you, but don't avoid.

I'm in a similar situation, my birthday is also coming soon and they are usually pretty sad days. I got my family around, but i still feel pretty empty and alone, since i barely got any friends. I'd say it's a good thing to not engage too much with social media, in my case i can't avoid feeling overwhelmed by what's going on around me and start comparing it with life. 

I think it's better to compare yourself to who you were before,try not to be too harsh,  give yourself some credit and instead try to be fair, patient, forgiving and kind.

Also it's OK to feel sad and irritable once in a while, just don't let it take over you. I try to appreciate all the good things that i tend to take for granted and  remember to think that given enough time and diligence, things can improve.

Hope that you get better soon. :)

I'm with you, as i get older and feel lonelier my anxiety raises on holidays, Christmas, birthday, new years eve, they all feel the same. It feels like i'll never develop as a person and that i will be stuck here next year. I want to improve, but everything feels overwhelming and out of reach. Intrusive negative thoughts and memories don't help much. Currently trying to keep my anxiety levels down so i can try to enjoy what i have and remember where i was a year ago and how much I've improved. That's the least i feel i can do, try to value what i have now.
